### 4. Least-squares physics-informed neural approximation

#### 4.1. Hard initial-condition ansatz

The neural approximation used for the reported tables is \[u_\theta(x,t)=u_0(x)+t\sum_{m=1}^{M}c_m\phi_m(x,t), \label{eq:hardansatz} \tag{21}\] where \[\phi_m(x,t)=\tanh(a_m\widehat{x}+b_m\widehat{t}+d_m), \qquad \widehat{x}=2x-1, \qquad \widehat{t}=2t/T-1. \tag{22}\]

The factor \(t\) enforces \(u_\theta(x,0)=u_0(x)\) exactly. Consequently, the initial condition is not included as an active loss term in the hard-constrained runs. It is monitored separately through \[D_{\text{IC}}=\left(\frac{1}{N_{\text{IC}}}\sum_i |u_\theta(x_i,0)-u_0(x_i)|^2\right)^{1/2}, \tag{23}\] which is zero up to roundoff for (21).

The hidden-feature parameters \((a_m,b_m,d_m)\) are sampled independently for each seed, with \(a_m,b_m\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1.5^2)\) and \(d_m\sim\mathcal{U}[-1,1]\). Only the output coefficients \(c_m\) are solved. This random-feature formulation is more restrictive than a fully trainable deep PINN, but it is appropriate for a linear benchmark study because it produces a reproducible residual-minimizing approximation without the confounding influence of optimizer trajectories.

#### 4.2. Residual equations and least-squares system

The interior residual is \[r_f(x,t)=\partial_tu_\theta(x,t)-\alpha\partial_{xx}u_\theta(x,t). \tag{24}\]

The endpoint residuals are \[ r_0(t) =\partial_tu_\theta(0,t)+ku_\theta(0,t)+\beta\partial_xu_\theta(0,t)-g_0(t),\label{eq:r0}\ \tag{25}\] \[r_1(t) =\partial_tu_\theta(1,t)+ku_\theta(1,t)-\beta\partial_xu_\theta(1,t)-g_1(t).\label{eq:r1} \ \tag{26}\]

Because (21) is linear in the unknown vector \( c=(c_1,\ldots,c_M)^T\), collocation of \(r_f\), \(r_0\), and \(r_1\) leads to a linear least-squares problem \[ c=\arg\min_{ z\in\mathbb{R}^M}\left\|A z- b\right\|_2^2+\lambda\| z\|_2^2, \label{eq:ridge} \tag{27}\] where \(\lambda=10^{-8}\) in all reported runs. The ridge term regularizes the normal equations while remaining small relative to the residual scales.

For each random-feature seed, the collocation set contains \(2000\) pseudorandom interior points and a \(44\times45\) tensor-product interior grid, giving \(N_f=3980\) interior collocation points. The boundary residuals are collocated at \(401\) equally spaced times per endpoint. Unless otherwise stated, \(M=250\) hidden features are used. All reported solution errors are computed on an independent \(301\times301\) evaluation grid. PDE residual RMS values are computed on \(12000\) evaluation points sampled from that grid, and boundary residual RMS values are computed on \(2001\) equally spaced boundary times.

### 6. Error and residual metrics

For a computed approximation \(u_h\), the reported relative errors are \[E_{L^2}=\frac{\|u_h-u^\ast\|_{L^2([0,1]\times[0,T])}}{\|u^\ast\|_{L^2([0,1]\times[0,T])}}, \qquad E_{L^\infty}=\frac{\|u_h-u^\ast\|_{L^\infty([0,1]\times[0,T])}}{\|u^\ast\|_{L^\infty([0,1]\times[0,T])}}. \tag{35}\]

The continuous norms are approximated by uniform-grid quadrature or evaluation on the stated grids. Residual magnitudes are reported as \[R_f=\left(\frac{1}{N_q}\sum_{i=1}^{N_q}|r_f(x_i,t_i)|^2\right)^{1/2}, \qquad R_j=\left(\frac{1}{N_b}\sum_{i=1}^{N_b}|r_j(t_i)|^2\right)^{1/2}, \quad j=0,1. \tag{36}\]

These metrics are reported explicitly to avoid the limitations of figure-only assessment.

### 7. Numerical results

#### 7.1. Five-seed neural benchmark results

Table 2 reports five-seed statistics for Benchmarks A and B. Benchmark A is solved with homogeneous boundary forcing under the compatibility condition \(k=\pi^2\). Benchmark B uses the fully active forcing (20). The statistics are computed over seeds \(s=0,1,2,3,4\).

The principal numerical observation is that Benchmark B is not only specified analytically but also solved and evaluated quantitatively. Its relative errors remain below \(10^{-6}\), while the RMS boundary residuals remain below \(10^{-5}\). Because \(u_x(0,t)\) and \(u_x(1,t)\) are nonzero in Benchmark B, these residuals test the active \(\beta u_x\) contribution in (3)–(4). Benchmark A produces larger errors and residuals than Benchmark B in the present implementation, primarily because the faster decay \(\mathrm{e}^{-\pi^2t}\) is more demanding for the fixed random-feature set than the milder decay \(\mathrm{e}^{-\pi^2t/4}\) in Benchmark B. Nevertheless, both cases display small relative errors and stable seed-to-seed behavior.

Figure 2 shows representative exact time traces for Benchmark B at several spatial locations. The figure highlights the smooth temporal decay and the variation in amplitude across the interval, which together make Benchmark B a useful complementary test to the flux-inactive cosine benchmark.

Table A5 probes one component of the SOAP update. SOAP accumulates Kronecker factors from the gradients, computes an eigenbasis from them, and runs an Adam-style update in that basis. The refresh period n governs how often the eigendecomposition is redone; the Kronecker factors and the second moments are updated at every step regardless of n, so the sweep varies the currency of the basis and not the amount of curvature information available. The ablation supports a robustness result: SOAP remains broadly reliable across the tested refresh periods, with n=50 the weakest of them. It does not apportion the benefit between the curvature information and the structured conditioning built from it since the two are not varied independently here and the Adam baseline differs from SOAP in learning rate and schedule as well as in the form of its preconditioner. A separation of that kind would require matched controls at identical learning rate and moment parameters, substituting an identity, frozen, or random basis for the one SOAP computes, which we leave to future work.

# 

Research paper

An adaptive residual-structured and scheduled loss weighting framework for enhancing physics-informed neural networks in solving partial differential equations

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cnsns.2025.109531Get rights and content

## Highlights

  * •

An adaptive Physics-Informed Residual Neural Network (aPIRNN) has been proposed.

  * •

Adaptive residual connections are introduced to alleviate the vanishing gradients.

  * •

Efficiency has been improved by introducing a scheduled loss weighting mechanism.

  * •

Incorporated a higher-order adaptive optimizer, SOAP, to accelerate the optimization.

  * •

aPIRNN outperformed recent variants of PINN, including PIKAN, for many problems.

  * •

Investigated the impact of using mixed-precision training for PINNs.

## Abstract

In this work, we introduce an adaptive Physics-Informed Residual Neural Network (aPIRNN) that enhances the performance of the physics-informed neural network (PINN) by combining an adaptive residual network (ResNet) architecture with an epoch-dependent scheduled loss weighting strategy to solve partial differential equations (PDEs). The proposed model mitigates the challenges faced by PINN due to architectural limitations, cost function formulation leading to training imbalance between various residual terms, and also due to the nature of the governing differential equations. The adaptive residual structure improves the flow of the gradient and the representation of the solution, while dynamic weighting of the loss function components helps improve the training imbalance in the loss function. In addition, we incorporate a second-order adaptive optimizer, Shampoo with Adam in the Preconditioner eigenbasis (SOAP) in aPIRNN, to further accelerate the optimization. Our comprehensive illustration using benchmark PDEs demonstrates that aPIRNN outperforms conventional PINN, Physics-Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (PIKAN), and recent variants of PINN. In addition, we investigated the impact of mixed-precision training for PINNs.

## Introduction

Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) has emerged as a robust framework to learn and solve many scientific problems [1]. Also, several operator-learning frameworks such as DeepONet, Fourier Neural Operators, and their physics-in-loss variants have emerged as powerful alternatives, highlighting the broader importance of physics-constrained operator learning for PDEs [9], [20]. To mitigate the challenges arising from network architectures, residual connections [21] are incorporated. If the issues are due to loss functions, strategies like weighted loss terms, learning rate annealing [10], augmented Lagrangian methods [22], and self-adaptive PINNs [23] were introduced. Apart from the common practice of using a combination of Adam and Limited-memory Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (L-BFGS) optimization in the PINN framework, other novel optimization algorithms such as Shampoo [24], and its recent improvement, SOAP [25], are considered. SOAP retains the same idea of Shampoo’s dimension-wise preconditioning, but utilizes eigen-decomposition to rotate gradients, applies simple element-wise Adam-style scaling, and then rotates back. Many other studies attempt to explain the failure of PINNs and try to tackle these challenges [10], [11], [21], [26].

In this work, we propose a novel framework, an adaptive Physics-Informed Residual Neural Network (aPIRNN), that integrates an adaptive residual neural network architecture with a scheduled loss weight to improve the training dynamics of PINNs. The architecture incorporates skip connections within the feedforward neural network (FNN), which are learned jointly with the network weights. This facilitates more stable gradient propagation and accelerated convergence by preserving the features across layers. The proposed scheduled loss weighting mechanism dynamically adjusts the contributions of each loss term during the training, thereby mitigating optimization imbalance and enabling more efficient learning of both PDE residual and auxiliary constraints. We have also implemented the SOAP optimizer[25] in aPIRNN training and compared it with the commonly used Adam and LBFGS optimizers. Additionally, we analyze PINN performance under single and double floating-point precision and explore mixed-precision implementations to assess computational trade-offs.

The remaining part of this article is organized as follows: Section 2 outlines the key challenges associated with PINN training, illustrated through an example. Further, the section details the proposed aPIRNN model as a potential solution. Section 4 presents detailed numerical experiments on several benchmark examples, evaluating the performance of aPIRNN, both with and without the novel SOAP optimization method. Comparisons are made with the vanilla PINN, PIKAN, and, in selected cases, with other enhanced PINN variants. Finally, Section 5 concludes the article with a summary and closing remarks.

Sensitivity analysis using Physics-informed neural networks

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.engappai.2024.108764Get rights and content

## Abstract

The goal of this paper is to provide a simple approach to perform local sensitivity analysis using Physics-informed neural networks (PINN). The main idea lies in adding a new term in the loss function that regularizes the solution in a small neighborhood near the nominal value of the parameter of interest. The added term represents the derivative of the loss function with respect to the parameter of interest. The result of this modification is a solution to the problem along with the derivative of the solution with respect to the parameter of interest (the sensitivity). We call the new technique SA-PNN which stands for sensitivity analysis in PINN. The effectiveness of the technique is shown using four examples: the first one is a simple one-dimensional advection–diffusion problem to show the methodology, the second is a two-dimensional Poisson’s problem with nine parameters of interest, and the third and fourth examples are one and two-dimensional transient two-phase flow in porous media problem.

Abstract This paper studies an evolving bulk–surface finite element method for a model of tissue growth, which is a modification of the model of Eyles, King and Styles (2019, A tractable mathematical model for tissue growth. Interfaces Free Bound, 21, 463–493). The model couples a Poisson equation on the domain with a forced mean curvature flow of the free boundary, with nontrivial bulk–surface coupling in both the velocity law of the evolving surface and the boundary condition of the Poisson equation. The numerical method discretizes evolution equations for the mean curvature and the outer normal and it uses a harmonic extension of the surface velocity into the bulk. The discretization admits a convergence analysis in the case of continuous finite elements of a polynomial degree at least 2. The stability of the discretized bulk–surface coupling is a major concern. The error analysis combines stability estimates and consistency estimates to yield optimal-order $H^{1}$-norm error bounds for the computed tissue pressure and for the surface position, velocity, normal vector and mean curvature. Numerical experiments illustrate and complement the theoretical results.
